title: AI hyperscalers are transforming debt
paragraphs: Euan HealyandEmily Herbertin London andMichelle Chanin New York
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?
As Silicon Valley’s tech giants fan out across the world in search of cash, often changing the economic facts of life in the process, Europe’s debt markets are set to welcome a new borrower.
Meta will tap the European bond market for the first time this autumn to raise funds for its AI expansion, according to investors familiar with its goals.

It is due to be the latest stop in the sector’s record-breaking hunt for funds from new and old sources alike — a headlong rush with big implications for other borrowers during the current AI investment supercycle.

“The overarching narrative is — anywhere and everywhere,” says Greg Peters, co-chief investment officer of asset manager PGIM’s credit business. “The quantum of debt that is hitting the marketplace is historic. The numbers are just absolutely enormous. It’s transformational.”

The fundraising binge is changing the way the world borrows money, affecting where, when and at what cost companies and governments issue debt. Some have said it could be the biggest shift since the creation of the Eurobond market in the 1960s.

Many companies are now being forced to tiptoe around hyperscalers, timing their bond issues to avoid clashing with those of the tech giants and, investors say, often borrowing for shorter periods to avoid the market’s glut of long-term debt.

Even the very biggest financial players say they are affected.

Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh and US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent argue that the hyperscalers are competing for capital with the $31tn US Treasury market, where last week 10-year borrowing costs hit their highest since 2007.

Staff at the European Central Bank have expressed concern that “the surge in big tech borrowing could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance.” In a blog post last month, they asked: “Can euro area financial markets smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows?”

The scale of the borrowing has shattered precedents. Last week Japan’sSoftBank raised more than $11bn of debtin the biggest junk bond issue in history to finance an investment in ChatGPT creator OpenAI.
Overall, according to Goldman Sachs, investors have provided about $500bn of financing to AI-linked groups so far this year.

The hyperscalers — Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle — account for about $200bn of the total, and are expected to issue more than $1tn of new debt over the next few years to finance their vast investment in the infrastructure needed to power AI.
Meta did not respond to a request for comment about its plans to raise funds in Europe.

Such outsize demand has created credit markets that can support larger and longer-term debt issues than ever before. But it has distorted pricing, with highly rated bonds sometimes trading at discounts to lesser-quality issues because of the sudden glut in supply.

It also brings new risks. Chipmakers, data centre operators and their power providers are all borrowing from public and private credit markets as well as financing each other, making it hard for the pension funds and insurers who buy their debt to assess their true level of exposure to the sector.
The interconnections between borrowers, in a new sector whose long-term trajectory is still unclear, have sparked concerns that if one falters, others could be dragged down with it.

“Inevitably, this is a one-way bet,” says Scott Schulte, global co-head of investment-grade debt syndicate at Barclays. “As long as everything goes right, it’s good. But the minute there’s a problem anywhere . . . the ecosystem is so intertwined.”
In 2025, when hyperscaler debt issuance was just beginning, the tech giants set their bankers a challenge.

The question, according to Schulte, was: “How much debt do you think that we can issue over the course of the year?” They did not just mean in their home market, the world’s largest, he adds. They wanted to know how much they could possibly borrow “across currencies, globally”.
Their bankers spent that year “putting pencil to paper, and working out what [they] think the actual capacity is in any given market”, he says.
Then they acted, beginning with the market they know best, the $12tn US corporate bond market.

Fraser Lundie, global head of fixed income at Aviva Investors, says the ensuing “supply shock” quickly overwhelmed investors. With so much debt on offer, they were able to demand lower prices, meaning higher yields, or borrowing costs, for hyperscalers.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Lotfi Karoui, multi-asset credit strategist at Pimco, adds that the “repricing” in hyperscaler bonds — in some cases, close to levels of junk or lower-quality bonds — is occurring “because the pipeline is too unpredictable right now”.

During the second-quarter earnings season, Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta increased their projections for this year’s capital spending to a combined $745bn. “We haven’t found a landing zone for capex and supply . . . the pace and magnitude of revisions to capex are quite significant,” Karoui says.

So far, this repricing has mostly been confined to the tech names themselves. “At the moment you’ve almost got two credit markets, the AI-related issuers and everyone else,” says Andy Chorlton, chief investment officer for fixed income at M&G. But he is concerned that, over time, borrowing costs for all high-grade corporate issuers will be dragged higher. “That is something that we are certainly focused on.”

There have been few signs that higher financing costs are deterring the tech giants from issuing more debt, however. “Elon Musk is endeavouring to colonise Mars,” says PGIM’s Peters, referring to SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centres in space. “It doesn’t matter to him if a bunch of bond investors charge an extra hundred basis points.”
To avoid overwhelming the market, some hyperscalers have given investors assurances, for instance, that they will not issue debt in two consecutive quarters.

But companies in other sectors are still growing concerned that they will be crowded out by hyperscalers’ massive debt offerings. Coming to market at the same time as Oracle or Amazon could mean higher costs as bond buyers hold back cash to deploy in the AI-related issue.

David Brown, co-head of global investment-grade fixed income at asset manager Neuberger Berman, says that when a large AI issuance is coming to market, “we will definitely prepare . . . We will hold off or make sure we have capacity to add that issuance.”
The magnitude of the borrowing, and its impact on pricing even in the highly developed US bond market, has led the tech giants and their bankers to travel the world.
Records have tumbled as a result. In June, Amazon sold C$14bn ($10bn) of debt, smashing the Canadian currency’s previous record of C$8.5bn set by Alphabet just a few weeks earlier.

Canadian borrowers now have to make sure that they “are not going head to head with some of the bigger deals that are out there”, says Abeed Ramji, head of Canadian debt capital markets at TD Securities. “The windows of access matter so much more than they used to in the past.”

Ramji adds, however, that Canada’s ability to absorb large deals has helped promote the country as a strong credit market and encouraged other companies to increase the sizes of their own debt issues.
“I don’t think this takes away from any demand,” he says. “The pie is just getting bigger.”

Last month Alphabet issued a record A$5.5bn ($3.9bn) bond in Australia, more than twice as large as the previous biggest. The group also holds the record for the largest Swiss franc bond issue, having raised SFr3.1bn ($3.7bn) there in February. Amazon’s SFr2.8bn offering in May is the second-largest.
The deluge of debt in hitherto less sought-out markets is pushing up borrowing costs for other companies and prompting them to shift the timing or duration of their deals, investors said.

Barclays analysis of the European credit market found that non-hyperscaler bonds were underperforming in parts of the market where hyperscaler issuance has been heaviest, such as longer-dated, higher-rated bonds.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

The same appears true in Canada. Since Amazon and Alphabet’s record deals, the country’s highest-quality AA corporate credit index — where both hyperscalers sit — has traded at a discount to the equivalent index of A-rated bonds.

Even though hyperscaler deals can represent a meaningful share of current issuance in individual foreign-currency markets, their overall outstanding debt is a relatively small component of bond indices.

“When we look at the percentage of outstanding debt across the different markets, the euro capacity for hyperscaler debt is still untapped,” says Rehan Latif, global head of credit trading at Morgan Stanley.

The new deals have revitalised some of the smaller markets, say bankers. Adam Bothamley, global head of debt capital markets at HSBC, says there had been a slower pipeline of companies seeking to borrow in pounds this year, until the hyperscalers stepped in. “Having these sizeable transactions has been really helpful and has increased interest in and focus on the sterling market,” he adds.

Alphabet sold £5.5bn worth of sterling bonds in February, part of a $31.5bn package that included a rare 100-year £1bn bond that some say rekindled interest in long-maturity sterling debt. Amazon also raised £4.25bn earlier this month, its first-ever sterling issue.

The unknowns of gobbling up new debt at such a long maturity are huge, some investors warn. “If you just take it at its face value, investors are buying up to 100 years of unsecured debt in a transformational technology,” says Peters of PGIM. “Not to overly simplify it, but 100 years is a long time. I don’t think it’s good risk reward . . . it’s unknowable.”

Christian Hantel, head of global corporate bonds at Swiss bank Vontobel, highlights the practicalities of piling into smaller debt markets. “Those local markets will be filled quicker than the dollar market,” he says. “In some smaller markets like Swiss, sterling, Canadian, the market is getting close to its limit soon.”

The AI debt spree comes at a fragile moment for bond investors globally, as borrowing costs for governments in mature economies such as the US, UK, Germany and France rise to levels last seen in the late-2000s.
Whether investors have cashed out of government debt to buy into bonds issued by tech giants, as some credit-watchers have asserted, is a hot debate on Wall Street.
“We can see clearly . . . [hyperscaler debt] competes with government bonds,” says Marion Le Morhedec, chief investment officer for fixed income at Fidelity International.

“As a portfolio manager . . . that question about whether to invest in a 30-year bond from a hyperscaler versus a government is relevant, where it wasn’t before,” she adds. The hyperscalers offer an attractive “pure credit story”, as investors grow less tolerant of governments’ inability to rein in deficits and spending.
Others are less sure, arguing that the sell-off in government bonds has principally been due to macroeconomic factors such as inflation and fiscal deficits.

“The numbers we are talking about on the sovereign side are so much higher,” said HSBC’s Bothamley. “It’s a stretch to say that . . . hyperscaler issuance is causing any sustained increase in [sovereign] yields.”

It is difficult to prove that investors are ditching government bonds for corporate debt. But markets have nevertheless been jolted by the arrival of such large and relatively price-insensitive sellers of debt, at a time when some traditional bond buyers — notably central banks and defined-contribution pension funds — have reined in their purchases.

“As heavy government borrowing collides with growing AI financing needs . . . persistent demand for capital is one reason we think borrowing costs can stay elevated,” BlackRock analysts wrote last week.

Matthew Hornbach, global head of macro strategy at Morgan Stanley, adds that part of the sell-off of US Treasuries that has pushed up yields could be down to banks or brokers hedging their hyperscaler credit exposure. When such companies provide liquidity for investors to buy and sell previously issued bonds, they are known as primary dealers.
“We can find a small amount of evidence, through US primary dealer balance sheet holdings of corporate bonds”, that hyperscaler issuance is having an effect on US Treasury yields, Hornbach says.

Even so, some investors think the authorities in charge of governments’ debt-issuing plans are having to think harder about when they conduct debt auctions, to avoid competing with a popular hyperscaler deal.

“We are starting to see countries thinking about AI issuance, going shorter or avoiding timing when they think there will be AI issuance,” says Henrietta Pacquement, chief operating officer for fixed income at Allspring Global Investments.
As the AI-related share of credit markets grows around the world, so do the risks associated with a downturn in the sector that now influences all other capital markets to some degree.

Although the majority of AI’s debt needs are being met in the safer investment-grade market, the sector’s more speculative names such as cloud-computing company CoreWeave have been venturing into the market for junk debt.

Such riskier issuers are deeply intertwined with the rest of the AI ecosystem. “If something did break in the below-investment-grade market, either a credit or a specific data centre, that would not play well in investment grade,” says Brown, at Neuberger.
With tech giants tapping all corners of the financial market for capital, assessing the overall exposure to individual borrowers has also become increasingly difficult.
Meta, for instance, has issued various bonds through its corporate balance sheet and via special-purpose vehicles tied to individual data centre projects.

Loren Moran, fixed-income portfolio manager at Wellington Management, says that “people have crept higher on single-issuer limits than they’ve really accounted for” and that close monitoring is needed across asset classes to avoid being unintentionally overweight on a single name.

With so much money committed to the bet that AI will transform the global economy to the benefit of the hyperscalers and their investors, a sector slowdown could come with huge financial consequences.
“The credit story in hyperscalers rests on a single consensus assumption, that operating cash flow triples from $600bn to $2tn,” Apollo’s chief economist, Torsten Sløk, wrote this month.
“If this doesn’t happen, then the risk is that the AI trade weakens, with credit spreads widening, capex plans getting cut and ultimately US GDP growth slowing,” Sløk warned.

Leading AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI have already talked of slowing development after rogue AI agents hacked into websites. Popular opposition to power-hungry data centres is growing, especially in the US. It is far from clear what the long-term financial returns from AI will be, or which companies will reap them. Analogies with the bust that followed the railway boom of the 19th century, which was also capital-intensive and largely debt-financed, are commonplace.

In the wake of mounting worries by equity investors that the world’s stock markets are dangerously tied to the fortunes of AI, the same risk is creeping into the bond market — risking an even bigger fallout if cracks emerge.

“New bonds . . . are increasingly a claim on the same AI investment cycle that has been driving equity return,” says Lucas Baynes, a senior investment strategist at Vanguard. In other words, the places investors can hide from the financial consequences of AI are getting fewer and further between.

title: Why investors think Panama will overcome Trump threats
paragraphs: Christine Murrayin Mexico City andJoseph Cotterillin London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Foreign investors have been buying up Panama’s debt, betting that the Central American country can stage a remarkable recovery from a recent political and social crisis that threatened to badly damage its economy.

Despitemass proteststhat closed its largest foreign investment — a copper mine accounting for 5 per cent of GDP — and deterred other investors, followed by a threat by US President Donald Trump last year to “take back” the Panama Canal, Panama’s bonds have performed much better than many investors had expected.
The premium over US Treasuries it pays to borrow has dropped from as much as 3.5 percentage points in 2023 and 2024 to about 1.5 percentage points, in a sign of demand for the bonds.
Finance minister Felipe Chapman told the FT that, while it would take time for some policies to take effect, the government’s fiscal restraint had helped lure back investors.
“You have to first put the house in order, physically speaking, then you have to reconstruct or rebuild confidence and trust,” he said.

“The last time we went to the global market was in February and I was personally expecting a premium of about 160 [basis points, or 1.6 percentage points], now we closed at about 145,” he said. “So it was awesome, we’re very happy.”

Panama’s long-dated dollar bonds currently trade at yields of 6 to 6.5 per cent, below the bonds of higher-rated US AI companies such as Meta, although countries such as Chile, Guatemala and Peru have smaller risk premiums over Treasuries.

Its economy has accelerated this year after a sharp slowdown, growing 6.4 per cent year on year in the second quarter after 4.8 per cent in the first quarter, ranking it as one of the fastest-growing in the region. A wide range of sectors have shared in the growth, including construction and tourism, as well as more activity around the country’s canal after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
“A few quarters ago a sort of abyss was at the nation’s doorstep,” said UBS analyst Alberto Rojas in a recent note. “That is no longer the case; now the good times are starting to roll in.”

For decades, Panama was considered the poster child of Latin America among investors, with high growth, relatively solid institutions and a business-friendly environment. In 2018, it became a high-income economy under World Bank definitions, joining a small club of just three other nations in Latin America, with aspirations to become the “Singapore of Latin America” as a prosperous finance and trading hub.

But social discontent over government corruption and huge inequality exploded into protests in 2023 thatshut down the copper mine, which is owned by Canada’s First Quantum and which had been expected to add billions of dollars in royalties to the country’s coffers and boost economic growth. In 2025, separate protests over pension reform shut downbanana plantationsowned by Chiquita Brands.

That spooked investors and led to a sharp sell-off in government debt. Fitch downgraded the country’s bonds to junk territory in 2024, although S&P Global and Moody’s have kept Panama on the lowest rungs of investment grade.

However, President José Raúl Mulino’s government cut the deficit from more than 6 per cent in 2024 to 3.7 per cent last year, and it has since narrowed further. Officials also increased the proportion of government financing coming from bank loans and multilateral institutions, while a bond sale in February was more than four times oversubscribed.
“At the very beginning, I didn’t get a phone call,” Chapman said, referring to foreign interest in investing in the country. “Now, I don’t have time to receive all the people who want to come.”
Concerns over further downgrades to Panama’s credit have faded, said Jeff Grills, a portfolio manager at Aegon Asset Management, which holds Panamanian bonds.

title: The bargain between shareholders and companies is being eroded
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?
The writer is chief executive of Norges Bank Investment Management
When you buy a share in a company, you enter into a bargain. You take the price as it comes, up or down, and in return you get a set of rights.
These include a vote on the decisions that matter, reliable information about the company, a fair share of the value created and a way to enforce the rights if they are denied.

Well, at least this is how it used to be. This bargain is now being rewritten. Not in one market but in many, across Asia, Europe and the Americas. Some 60 per cent of jurisdictions around the world now allow shares with unequal voting powers, up from 44 per cent in 2020, according to OECD figures from last year. And in the US, 36 per cent of new listings in the first half of 2026 had dual-class shares, the highest share recorded since the Council of Institutional Investors began tracking this in 2017.

As a long term-investor and owner of shares in more than 7,000 companies around the world, these developments worry us greatly. Why do we care so much? Because strong shareholder rights are profitable, not only for us but for the market as a whole.

Research indicates that strong shareholder rights go with deeper, more liquid markets and broader access to financing. Weakening them raises the cost of capital, and companies with stronger protections have historically traded at higher valuations.

Rights also create trust, and trust is what keeps long-term money invested when short-term money heads for the exit. We own a piece of almost every listed company across markets, and we cannot simply sell out. If those companies succeed, so do we. We share this interest with everyone who depends on healthy markets — savers, pensioners and businesses that need capital to grow.

What is it that worries us? First of all, the vote is being diluted. More companies are listing with two share classes so that the largest owners can retain control. Such structures can attract founders to go public, which is something we encourage. However, over time each share should carry equal say.

Second, reporting requirements are under pressure in several markets. Shareholders cannot see inside a company or tell whether it is run in their interest. They depend on what companies disclose. The limiting of any reporting cost that serves no one is something we welcome (andhave argued forin the past), but removing public information that shareholders rely on is not.

Third, shareholders have a right to a share of any payout in proportion to what they own. They should be protected from transactions that move value to a controlling shareholder or to management at their expense. But safeguards against such transactions are being weakened in several markets, leaving shareholders with fewer ways to identify and challenge them.

And finally, we see that access to the courts is narrowing. A right is only as good as the means to enforce it. Shareholders should be able to choose where to bring a claim and pursue it without excessive cost or delay. Safeguards against meaningless lawsuits are reasonable but safeguards that also block claims with merit and weaken protection for all shareholders are not.
Each of these changes may appear reasonable on its own, but together they represent a concerning weakening of shareholder rights.

We want more companies to come to the market, not fewer. So, we believe that listing should not be made needlessly burdensome. But there is a trade-off. Competition between financial centres should not turn into competition to offer investors the least.

We love speed and we love a great race. But not one that could easily turn out to be a race to the bottom. Everyone in the market has a role and an interest in protecting these rights. But no one can protect these rights alone.

Regulators should keep their frameworks steady, which is itself a form of investor protection. Exchanges should hold the governance line they set, even when competition for listings pushes the other way. Index providers should give governance real weight in their inclusion rules, which now decide what many investors end up owning. Boards should protect shareholder rights through the governance choices they make, including where to incorporate and list. Finally, investors should use their own rights and back the efforts to defend them.
The bargain on buying shares was built on the back of strong shareholder rights. It will not hold together unless we all step up.

Good morning. So far, a 10-year Treasury yield of 5.2 per cent doesn’t bother US stocks. The S&P 500 rose Friday and remains right in the trading range it has been in since the beginning of August, when the yield was 4.6 per cent. That economic growth is a major driver of the yield increase certainly helps. The big risk, as we described on thepodcastlast week, is that the rapid rise in yields causes some sort of financial accident. But maybe we’ll get lucky!
Usually we run interviews on Fridays but the bond market excitement disrupted our plans. Email us:[email protected].

Helen Thompson is professor of political economy at the University of Cambridge and the author ofDisorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century. Her work focuses on energy, geopolitics and the economic pressures reshaping western democracies. She spoke toUnhedgedearlier this month about the latest energy shock, China and US energy power, high debt levels and the politics of central bank independence. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.
Unhedged:During the post-pandemic inflation surge, people reached for historical analogies to understand that moment. What analogies explain the current energy shock?

Helen Thompson:In the 2021-22 energy shock there were some parallels with the 1970s. In both periods western countries had become accustomed to relatively low oil prices and experienced considerable domestic problems that arose not just from the high energy prices but also from the geopolitical conditions that caused it.

But the parallel that should have been drawn was to the oil price shock from 2005-08, which I think is underestimated in the history of the past couple of decades. A great deal of that was China’s demand for oil. Likewise, the beginning of the gas shock in 2021-22 wasn’t Russia’s invasion of Ukraine but China’s demand for liquefied natural gas which surged in the autumn of 2021. So actually the parallel is one of western countries having to adjust to China’s energy demand, which they haven’t been very good at over this century.
Unhedged:What makes the latest energy shock structural rather than temporary?

Thompson:From the late 1970s the US took responsibility for guaranteeing maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and out into the Persian Gulf. While the US had problems projecting military power in the Middle East, it has not had a problem acting as that guarantor. Now we’re seeing the US willing to accept turmoil around transit through the Gulf for months on end and, to some extent, being part of the reason why, given the blockade it imposed on some ships coming out of the Gulf.

I don’t think we’re ever really going back to a world in which the US acting as a guarantor of passage through the Strait of Hormuz can be taken for granted. And you can see that in the way in which various Arab states, including Saudi Arabia, are working on the presumption that they need pipelines. You are going to see Arab states really trying to move as far away as they can from reliance on maritime passage through that body of water.
Unhedged:Why has the global economy proved more resilient to the oil shock than expected?

Thompson:First, I think a large part of it is China’s demand destruction. China, in some sense, did prepare, if not exactly for this war, then for a similar war, given the amount of oil stockpiling that it did. The Chinese leadership have a quite good understanding of the geopolitical risks around their energy security and have taken that a lot more seriously than European countries have.

Second, the drawdowns from the US shouldn’t be underestimated in the explanation. But something that has surprised me is the ability of US producers to supply European countries with refined petroleum products. I think it suggests there’s more flexibility in the shale industry than might have been expected.
Unhedged:Many of the advanced economies are facing extraordinary debt levels and high borrowing costs. Do you think this will lead to financial repression?

Thompson:I think that’s been the direction of travel for some time. In a way, quantitative easing is a form of financial repression. It’s obviously very different from trying to directly cap yields but you’re still using the power of the central bank to support debt and keep yields low. QE has gone away but the need to sustain high levels of debt hasn’t gone away and in some cases it has got worse. So you are going to have something to replace what QE was doing.

The more formal ways of doing financial repression are just harder than they were before. They run into the hard constraints that international capital flows have imposed on the world economy since the 1970s — 1980s. We’re in quite uncertain territory because the ways in which the problem [of high debt levels] has been dealt with in the past are not really workable any longer. So I think we’re going to see lots of improvisation to achieve the same ends, which is sort of what Bessent has been trying to do.
Unhedged:Do you see any overall coherence to the Trump administration’s economic policy?

Thompson:I think that there is actually more rationality than there may seem. What I think is clear in the US, and what you can see in [Stephen Miran’s]Mar-a-Lago accordpaper, that for some of the people who have been economic advisers to Trump is the idea that US has a fundamental debt problem, the trajectory of the debt is unsustainable, and one of the reasons it’s unsustainable is because the interest on it is too high. I think we can see that they want to make the US debt more sustainable by paying less interest on it. And they will try to go about that through different means, some more strategic, some tactical. Whether that can succeed is a whole other question.
Unhedged:Is the 1990s conception of central bank independence still suited to the current political and economic challenges?
Thompson:It seems to me that you get a change in what the relationship is between politics and monetary policy at different economic and political junctures.

Central banks like the BoE were given independence against a relatively benign international monetary background. If you told them to keep inflation to 2 per cent or lower, that was both doable and didn’t come with hard trade-offs. I think that era ended with the crash. And, actually, we did get a political version of monetary policy. It just didn’t look how it had looked in the past because it was QE. But once QE has become so hard, what do you do now? I don’t think anybody really knows the answer. But I think [political monetary policy] is what you would expect once you’ve gone back to an underlying international monetary and financial order that is much less benign than the one that prevailed when the BoE was given its independence.

There’s almost a kind of “end of history” — type argument around the BoE’s independence. It was somehow the liberal thing to do. It’s what competent technocratic politics was when big ideological conflict was over. But it’s just as historically specific to that time period as the whole universal liberal democracy argument.

title: Australia’s biggest gold miner rejects $27bn takeover bid
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Elliott Management has called on Australia’s largest gold producer to hold fresh talks with its potential suitor after the company rejected an A$39bn ($27bn) takeover offer from South Africa’s Gold Fields that would create the world’s second-largest miner of the precious metal.
The future of Northern Star Resources has been uncertain since US hedge fund Elliott called for the Perth-based gold producer toput itself up for salein June following a series of profit warnings.
Gold Fields, which was identified by Elliott as one of the only gold producers large enough to buy the company, has approached its rival on multiple occasions in recent months.

Northern Star said on Monday that it had rejected an offer from Gold Fields, one of the world’s largestgoldproducers and which already has significant operations in Australia, as “opportunistic, unsolicited and conditional”.

Shares in Northern Star gained 7 per cent in Sydney, valuing the company at A$34bn ($23.8bn) — although the share price of about A$23.47 still trailed the implied A$27-a-share value of the rejected Gold Fields offer.

John Pike, a partner at Elliott, urged Northern Star to hold talks with Gold Fields. “We believe there’s immense potential for value creation at Northern Star, and any transaction would need to reflect that,” he said in a statement.
“But others clearly see the value here too, and we think the board has an obligation to engage with any serious buyer and fully evaluate the best path to deliver on that potential.”
Shares in Gold Fields fell 12 per cent in morning trading in Johannesburg, bringing the stock’s decline this year to almost a fifth.
A combination with Gold Fields, which owns four of Australia’s largest gold mines including Gruyere and Granny Smith, would be second globally to Newmont.
It would also create Australia’s largest gold miner with an annual output of 2.4mn ounces from the country. The combined company would derive almost 60 per cent of its gold from Western Australia.

title: TotalEnergies boosts buybacks and dividends as oil prices surge
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

TotalEnergies raised its share buyback target for the fourth quarter and promised to increase dividends by more than 5 per cent annually until the end of the decade as the French major profits from soaring oil and gas prices.

Though Total’s oil and gas production was hit by theIran-US warthat began in February, the group is among those now receiving a boost from high prices and refining margins, while its output is also growing in other regions.
The company said on Monday that it now aimed for share buybacks of $2.5bn in the fourth quarter and between $2bn and $2.5bn in the first quarter of 2027.

That is up from $1.5bn in the July to September period, and marks a notable turnaround from late last year when, like its peers, Total was damping its outlook and warning of lower returns. Brent crude prices were then below $70 a barrel, compared with the current figure of above $100 a barrel.
Total chief executive Patrick Pouyanné said the outlook was a turnaround from the period before the Iran war “when everyone was very bearish”.
“We’ll increase the buyback in two steps” so as not do “$4bn in one quarter”, he told analysts. “There’s room for high returns to shareholders.”

Total said it would increase its dividend by more than 5 per cent a year between 2026 and 2030, while strongly increasing its free cash flow and reducing debt. The group also forecast a boom ahead for its electricity production, as it continues a pivot intorenewable energy, saying electric power would be 20 per cent of its energy mix by 2030.

“We say more oil and gas and more power,” Pouyanné said, acknowledging that the group was not looking to stop fossil-fuel investments for now even as it turned to electricity, which has drawn some criticism from activists.

Its update comes as higher prices at the pump risk sparking a political backlash, as opposition parties in France call for extra taxes on energy groups. The French government has rolled out targeted measures to help people relying on their cars for work, or on very modest wages, but has held off backing a windfall tax on the sector.
Total has been subsidising prices at its forecourts for several months in an effort to head off criticism and ease the situation for motorists, though this in turn has irked other distributors.

The company has a series of new liquefied natural gas projects coming online in the coming years and is adding new oil investments, including in Namibia, Libya, Mozambique and Papua New Guinea, though some of these have been beset by problems in the past, including security issues.
“On the growth front, investors will need to be confident on execution given a number of challenging projects in the hopper,” said Biraj Borkhataria, analyst at RBC Capital Markets.
Total shares closed up 0.8 per cent at €80.86.

title: Bond sell-off deepens and oil rises as Iran-US deal hopes fade
paragraphs: Kate Duguidin New York andEmily HerbertandIan Smithin London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

US borrowing costs hit their highest level since the onset of the global financial crisis, as fading hopes of a deal between Washington and Tehran drove up oil prices and a sell-off in the Treasury market deepened.

Brent crude rose more than 4 per cent to a high of $108.83 a barrel on Monday, after US President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, leaving no clear path to ending the seven-month war. Oil prices pared the gains later and settled 0.9 per cent higher at $105.28.

The renewed selling pressure onUS Treasuriessent yields on 10-year bonds up as much as 0.09 percentage points to 5.27 per cent, the highest since June 2007. Yields have risen for five consecutive sessions and are up more than 0.5 percentage points since mid-August, when Treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced an expanded bond buyback programme designed to calm the market.
The interest rate-sensitive US two-year yield also rose on Monday to 4.96 per cent, a 28-month high. Yields on both instruments backed off the highs in Monday afternoon trading.

“The potential fallout on the global economy from the war with Iran remains a key driver of the macro narrative,” said Ian Lyngen, head of US interest rate strategy at BMO Capital Markets. “There will, eventually, come a point at which the moves in energy will no longer have such an impact on US rates. Clearly, the market has yet to reach such an inflection point.”

Lyngen said that selling pressure on the 10-year Treasury could push its yield beyond 5.35 per cent before investors are incentivised to jump back into the market. Yields around that level would be at their highest in almost a quarter-century.
The rise in bond yields and oil prices also weighed on stocks, with the S&P 500 closing 0.8 per cent lower and the Nasdaq 100 dropping 1.1 per cent.

US borrowing costs have soared in recent weeks to levels not seen since before the global financial crisis, as signs of persistent inflation and strong growth in the world’s biggest economy have prompted investors to bet on higher interest rates.

The jump in yields has also pushed US mortgage rates above 7 per cent, as the bond sell-off translates into higher borrowing costs for Americans — just weeks before crucial midterm elections in which the country’s affordability crisis has become a central issue.
US voters have soured on Trump’s handling of the economy, sending his approval ratingssharply lower. Polls reveal deep voter disquiet about his war in Iran and its costs.

The Federal Reserve raised borrowing costs earlier this month for the first time since 2023, and investors in futures markets are betting on two more quarter-point rises by January — a marked shift from the cuts that had been expected before theUS-Iran warsent energy prices soaring.

Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chair of research at Barclays, said there was “nothing magical about these yield levels”, and it would take something substantial to reverse the sell-off, such as “if the US economy starts to slow down” or higher rates start “biting” risky assets such as stocks. “That would be one sign that we have perhaps gone far enough.”
UK government bonds also weakened further on Monday, with the 10-year gilt yield rising to 5.44 per cent — its highest level since 2007.
The sell-off on Monday also pushed French and Italian 10-year bond yields to fresh multiyear highs, with French borrowing costs at their highest level since 2008.
Other big central banks are also expected to make a series of rate rises in the coming months to contain a burst of inflation set off by the conflict.

Pooja Kumra, a rates strategist at TD Securities, said the bond sell-off was being powered by a combination of “persistent economic resilience” and the lack of a roadmap to “how the war might be resolved”, which was pushing investors to bet on rates remaining higher for longer.

Paul Watters, head of European credit research at S&P Global Ratings, said: “Our sense is that [bond] yields could grind higher” from here, in part because “we see the energy price shock continuing through 2027”.
“The buffers are eroding” in global energy reserves, Watters pointed out, referring to countries using up their stockpiles.

title: Burford Capital could gain up to $1.4bn from Apple patent defeat
paragraphs: Stefania Palmain London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Litigation funder Burford Capital said it stands to gain up to $1.4bn after a US federal jury ruled against Apple in a major technology patent case.
Burford on Monday said it had a “financial entitlement” in what it described as “one of the largest patent verdicts in US history”, sending shares up 9 per cent in early trading in London.

A jury in a San Diego court on Friday awarded $5.7bn in damages to Taction Technology, which develops vibration technology for electronic devices, and which sued Apple in 2021 for allegedly using its “patented inventions without license or authority”.

Taction accusedAppleof violating two of its patents concerning the haptic feedback in iPhones and Apple Watches in its legal complaint, alleging that the tech giant had capitalised on its “innovation and success” by selling the devices.

The company argued that Apple’s “Taptic Engine,” which is embedded in many of its products, unlawfully used its inventions. Apple denied the claim as “invalid” in its own legal filings, arguing that Taction had introduced insufficient evidence and rejecting accusations of wilful or indirect infringement.

Apple has pledged to appeal against the verdict and said in a statement: “While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today’s verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts.”

It added that its Taptic Engine was “fundamentally different from Taction’s technology, which Taction’s own testing of Apple’s products confirmed during trial.” Taction did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Taction’s win on Friday follows abig lossfor Burford in March, when a US appeals court overturned a ruling that found Argentina liable to pay $16bn to former shareholders of the oil major YPF.

The litigation funder had backed the shareholders’ claims and would have taken a share of the award. Its shares fell as much as 54 per cent in New York in the wake of the ruling — at the time its biggest intraday decline since July 2020.

Burfordon Monday cautioned that the Apple verdict did not “represent a final judgment or cash proceeds received by” the litigation funder. It said post-trial proceedings, including efforts by Apple to overturn the jury’s verdict, could leave Burford recovering “substantially less” than $1.4bn or, “in certain circumstances, [incurring] a total loss”.
“As with all litigation, the outcome remains uncertain until final resolution, and there can be no assurance as to the timing or amount of any ultimate recovery,” Burford added.

title: What is the AI capex breakeven rate?
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026

You might have heard that the AI hyperscalers are spending squillions on building data centres. The scale is now transforming debt markets, and not unreasonably this is raising some concerns about the boom’s durability.
As PGIM Fixed Income’s Greg Peters said in today’s (very good)FT Big Read:
The overarching narrative is — anywhere and everywhere. The quantum of debt that is hitting the marketplace is historic. The numbers are just absolutely enormous. It’s transformational.
Whether this is sustainable comes down to how much money these data centres are able to generate, and — ultimately — how much money AI as a whole will be able to generate.

Last month, Dan Davies crunched the numbers onAnthropic’s lease of SpaceX’s excess data centre capacityand concluded that data centre leasing is currently a wildly profitable business, even with extremely conservative assumptions on depreciation and construction costs.

But the calculus might look radically different when more compute comes online in the coming years, or, say, ifless compute-intensive open-models gain ground. So how much money do we all need to spend on AI tools for the hyperscaler capex splurge to actually make money?

Luckily, several economists have been crunching the numbers lately to figure out exactly this, albeit with subtly different perspectives and assumptions. Let’s start with Goldman Sachs’ estimates. In a report last week it said:

Outlook for AI capex:The largest US AI hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion in capex in 2026 and consensus expects $1.1 trillion in spending in 2027. Our baseline forecast is that capex spending will increase in 2027 and surpass consensus estimates but the rate of both capex growth and upside surprises will diminish relative to recent quarters.

What capex signals about required AI revenues:Based on average annual capex in 2026 and 2027, our equity analysts estimate that the hyperscalers need to generate annual AI revenues of roughly $300 billion in the next few years to break even on their investments. Hyperscaler cloud revenues have accelerated sharply this year, annualizing roughly $70 billion above the pre-AI trend in Q2 2026, and announced revenue backlogs exceed $1.5 trillion.

OK, so cloud computing AI revenues need to quickly increase by about 4x for the hyperscalers to simply break even on their investments. That seems punchy, but as Goldman points out, these revenues are now accelerating sharply.

However, to generate a return on investment capital of 30 per cent — at the lowest end of what the hyperscalers generated in the pre-hyperscale era — these data centres soon need to generate annual revenues of about $636bn. That’s more like 10x the current run rate.
Sure, the combined cloud revenue backlog of Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft is now $1.7tn, but Alphaville is a little less convinced by the firmness of this number than Goldman’s analysts.

Moreover, this is just what the underlying cloud-computing layer needs to generate. Then there are all the applications that sit on top of it, which presumably also want to actually make money at some point.

Goldman estimates that if these companies expect earnings margins of about 30 per cent — and the hyperscalers only generate a 10-20 per cent return on their capex — then the overall AI software spend is a bit over $1tn. Compared to a roughly $1.5tn global software spend, this seems ambitious but not fantastical.

However, if the hyperscalers are keen on a ROIC at least within touching distance of their historical norms, and AI software companies want margins closer to what software has historically generated, then consumer and enterprise spending needs to jump to nearly $2tn.

That seems . . . less feasible. Once consumers are used to a free or near-free product, hitting them with the full-fat cost of producing it is very difficult, as anyone experienced in the digital media industry can ruefully tell you.
On the same topic, here is afascinating recent paperby Columbia Business School’s Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.

Given the $8.2bn cost to build a 200-megawatt AI data centre — and the 183 gigawatts supposed to come online by 2032 — he estimates that the cumulative cost will clock in at over $10tn between 2025 and 2032 (which includes some spending on projects that will be finished after that point).

This is the equivalent of 3.6 per cent of GDP each year, a bigger capex splurge than those on canals, railroads, electricity and the internet in previous eras. “It would double the electricity consumption of the entire US residential sector,” Van Nieuwerburgh notes.

Assuming a modest 10 per cent unlevered return, a 50 per cent cash flow margin and a generous six-year life for the chips, he estimates that this will require annualised revenues of $3.7tn by 2032, or about 9.2 per cent of estimated US GDP at that point.
This is similar to the estimates of Jared Bernstein and Ryan Cummings, published in the former’sSubstacklast week:

Revenues would need to be between $2.4 trillion (if they simply broke even on the investments) and $3.8 trillion (if they needed to match the return they receive on their existing businesses) over the next six years. This is equivalent to their current incremental AI revenues increasing between 13-45 times in just six years (the range depends on revenue flow assumptions).

To make up for their relatively slow start, the hyperscalers need to quickly become hyper-profitable. Just in the next year, they’d need to post revenues between $520-850 billion, roughly three to four-and-a-half times what we estimate they made this year. If we strip out circular revenues—those from a firm in which the lab has an ownership stake—the future revenues must be even higher.

There are a lot of assumptions you could fiddle with to change the calculus, such as how firm the capex plans are, whether construction costs go up and down, token costs, the margin expectations of various layers in the AI ecosystem, demand from consumers and enterprise etc etc. Revenues are clearly growing at a remarkable rate right now, encouraging the optimists.
But the overall conclusion seems pretty clear: AI revenues very soon need to grow a LOT MORE for the size of these investment plans to make economic sense.

But the calculus might look radically different when more compute comes online in the coming years, or, say, ifless compute-intensive open-models gain ground. So how much money do we all need to spend on AI tools for the hyperscaler capex splurge to actually make money?

Luckily, several economists have been crunching the numbers lately to figure out exactly this, albeit with subtly different perspectives and assumptions. Let’s start with Goldman Sachs’ estimates. In a report last week it said:

Outlook for AI capex:The largest US AI hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion in capex in 2026 and consensus expects $1.1 trillion in spending in 2027. Our baseline forecast is that capex spending will increase in 2027 and surpass consensus estimates but the rate of both capex growth and upside surprises will diminish relative to recent quarters.

What capex signals about required AI revenues:Based on average annual capex in 2026 and 2027, our equity analysts estimate that the hyperscalers need to generate annual AI revenues of roughly $300 billion in the next few years to break even on their investments. Hyperscaler cloud revenues have accelerated sharply this year, annualizing roughly $70 billion above the pre-AI trend in Q2 2026, and announced revenue backlogs exceed $1.5 trillion.

OK, so cloud computing AI revenues need to quickly increase by about 4x for the hyperscalers to simply break even on their investments. That seems punchy, but as Goldman points out, these revenues are now accelerating sharply.

However, to generate a return on investment capital of 30 per cent — at the lowest end of what the hyperscalers generated in the pre-hyperscale era — these data centres soon need to generate annual revenues of about $636bn. That’s more like 10x the current run rate.

Sure, the combined cloud revenue backlog of Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft is now $1.7tn, but Alphaville is a little less convinced by the firmness of this number than Goldman’s analysts.

Moreover, this is just what the underlying cloud-computing layer needs to generate. Then there are all the applications that sit on top of it, which presumably also want to actually make money at some point.

Goldman estimates that if these companies expect earnings margins of about 30 per cent — and the hyperscalers only generate a 10-20 per cent return on their capex — then the overall AI software spend is a bit over $1tn. Compared to a roughly $1.5tn global software spend, this seems ambitious but not fantastical.

However, if the hyperscalers are keen on a ROIC at least within touching distance of their historical norms, and AI software companies want margins closer to what software has historically generated, then consumer and enterprise spending needs to jump to nearly $2tn.

That seems . . . less feasible. Once consumers are used to a free or near-free product, hitting them with the full-fat cost of producing it is very difficult, as anyone experienced in the digital media industry can ruefully tell you.

On the same topic, here is afascinating recent paperby Columbia Business School’s Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.

Given the $8.2bn cost to build a 200-megawatt AI data centre — and the 183 gigawatts supposed to come online by 2032 — he estimates that the cumulative cost will clock in at over $10tn between 2025 and 2032 (which includes some spending on projects that will be finished after that point).

This is the equivalent of 3.6 per cent of GDP each year, a bigger capex splurge than those on canals, railroads, electricity and the internet in previous eras. “It would double the electricity consumption of the entire US residential sector,” Van Nieuwerburgh notes.

Assuming a modest 10 per cent unlevered return, a 50 per cent cash flow margin and a generous six-year life for the chips, he estimates that this will require annualised revenues of $3.7tn by 2032, or about 9.2 per cent of estimated US GDP at that point.

This is similar to the estimates of Jared Bernstein and Ryan Cummings, published in the former’sSubstacklast week:

Revenues would need to be between $2.4 trillion (if they simply broke even on the investments) and $3.8 trillion (if they needed to match the return they receive on their existing businesses) over the next six years. This is equivalent to their current incremental AI revenues increasing between 13-45 times in just six years (the range depends on revenue flow assumptions).

To make up for their relatively slow start, the hyperscalers need to quickly become hyper-profitable. Just in the next year, they’d need to post revenues between $520-850 billion, roughly three to four-and-a-half times what we estimate they made this year. If we strip out circular revenues—those from a firm in which the lab has an ownership stake—the future revenues must be even higher.

There are a lot of assumptions you could fiddle with to change the calculus, such as how firm the capex plans are, whether construction costs go up and down, token costs, the margin expectations of various layers in the AI ecosystem, demand from consumers and enterprise etc etc. Revenues are clearly growing at a remarkable rate right now, encouraging the optimists.

But the overall conclusion seems pretty clear: AI revenues very soon need to grow a LOT MORE for the size of these investment plans to make economic sense.

title: Nvidia launches record $150bn share buyback
paragraphs: Tim Bradshawin London
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?
Nvidia is launching the biggest share buyback in US corporate history as the Silicon Valley chipmaker continues to reap huge profits from its perch at the top of the AI supply chain.
The world’s most valuable company said on Monday that its board had approved a $150bn increase to its buyback programme, eclipsing the record $110bn set by Apple in 2024.
Nvidiais now authorised to spend up to $235bn on share buybacks before January 2028.

Nvidia’s profits are surging as the tech industry continues to pour enormous sums into AI infrastructure, with Goldman Sachs forecasting that AI investment will exceed $1tn this year. Its chips are the workhorses of the large language models that power ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.

The company’s shares have risen more than 1,200 per cent since OpenAI debuted ChatGPT in late 2022. But the stock’s extraordinary momentum has slowed in 2026, rising about 20 per cent in the year to date, as more investors question the sustainability of the AI boom.
Shares in Nvidia jumped 3 per cent in early trading on Monday.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and chief executive, said on Monday that its new plan reflected “confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead” from AI.

“Nvidia’s growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing,” Huang said. “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders.”

Large buyback authorisations often indicate that a company’s management believes its shares are undervalued. But large capital returns are typically associated with a slowdown in growth for large, well-established companies.

When Apple announced its $110bn buyback in 2024, the iPhone maker held all of the top five spots for the largest such authorisations by a US company, according to Bloomberg. At the time, the iPhone’s growth was slowing but Apple continued to reap huge profits from its dominance of the smartphone market.

By contrast, Nvidia’s salescontinue to riserapidly. Its revenues are forecast to grow about 90 per cent this year. Fierce competitors in the AI race, including OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX, are all huge customers. Even Google, which has its own range of AI chips, is a big buyer of Nvidia’s products through its cloud computing unit.

Nvidia generated almost $100bn in free cash flow in its most recent financial year ending in January. That figure is forecast to more than triple to $329bn in fiscal 2028, according to consensus estimates from S&P Global’s Visible Alpha.
The chipmaker’s net income is forecast to more than double to $245bn in the current financial year, according to Visible Alpha, rising to $387bn in the following fiscal year ending in January 2028.

title: Meta launches enterprise AI business seeking to cash in on vast spending
paragraphs: Rafe Rosner-Uddinin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 28 2026

Meta is launching a new business selling AI tools to enterprise customers, as chief executive Mark Zuckerberg seeks new ways to generate returns from the company’s enormous investment in the technology.

The parent of Facebook and Instagram on Monday said that the new arm would bring together products including itsMuse personal assistantand coding tools, alongside access to its advanced AI models.Chirantan “CJ” Desai, chief executive of database group MongoDB, will helm the new business unit and report directly to Zuckerberg.

“We are starting the next major pillar of our business, Meta Enterprise Platform, to help businesses use AI to grow and transform in new ways as well,” said Zuckerberg in a statement.The move comes as Zuckerberg seeks to turn Meta’s vast spending on artificial intelligence into new sources of revenue beyond its core advertising business. The company plans to spend as much as $145bn in capital expenditure this year, much of it on the data centre infrastructure and advanced models underpinning its AI push.

Meta’sshares have rallied sharply in recent weeks as the success of Muse, its new AI assistant, has helped shift investor sentiment towards Zuckerberg’s spending spree. The app, the development of which was first revealed by the FT in May, has quickly become the most downloaded app on both the Apple and Android app stores in the US since its launch at the beginning of September.That rally reversed on Monday, with Meta shares falling 4 per cent following the announcement of its new enterprise arm. MongoDB shares dropped nearly 20 per cent after Desai’s departure was announced.Zuckerberg has insisted that Meta’s AI investments will bolster its core advertising business while creating new profit engines.
The easy-to-use Muse app offers consumers a team of autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks, such as ordering groceries, booking travel and organising finances.

Zuckerberg last week unveiled a new handheld AI “charm” device that will feature Muse, alongside a range of new capabilities including the ability to have live conversations with the interactive AI assistant.The Meta chief has previously discussed selling excess data centre capacity to customers, in a move that would see the company compete with cloud computing giants including Amazon and Microsoft.

On Monday, Zuckerberg told investors that the group would “use our strengths” including vast data centre infrastructure in a push to serve enterprise customers. He did not state whether the company had immediate plans to sell excess capacity to customers, similar to rival SpaceX, which has signed deals with Anthropic and Google.

“Meta Enterprise Platform will focus on turning its AI stack into products and services that companies can deploy for their own businesses,” Desai said. “Our goal is to make Meta the place enterprises come to scale their businesses.”

title: AMD to buy Fei-Fei Li’s AI start-up for $8bn
paragraphs: Michael Actonin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
UpdatedSeptember 28 2026

AMD has agreed to acquire AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li’s start-up World Labs for $8.2bn in an all-stock transaction that will push the Nvidia competitor further beyond chips into cutting-edge model development.

Li, the Stanford University researcher described as the “godmother of artificial intelligence”, founded the company in 2024 to work on so-called world models, AI systems that can understand and replicate 3D environments.
AMD’s chief executive Lisa Su said the deal would help the near-$1tn chip designer “shape its future technology road maps” by giving it insight into how the uses forAIare evolving.
BothAMDand its chief rival Nvidia are expanding beyond semiconductors into AI model development, using their huge earnings from hardware sales in recent years.

Nvidia, which builds its own models, earlier this month announced a $13bn deal to buy AI platform Hugging Face. It has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to start-up investments, debt guarantees and financial backstops across the AI sector.

AMD’s deal for San Francisco-based World Labs, which it expects to close by the end of 2026 pending regulatory approval, gives it a foothold in world models, which have potential applications in industries such as robotics and gaming.

World models, trained on images, video and text, are widely considered one of the next frontiers in AI beyond the large language models behind tools such as ChatGPT. Former Meta AI chief Yann LeCun left the company late last year to launchhis own start-upfocused on world models.

“Advancing the next generation of AI technology requires close collaboration across model research, systems and compute,” said Li. “Joining AMD will give our team the resources and engineering depth to accelerate our research and help define the infrastructure needed for the next era of AI.”
Li, who is best known for founding ImageNet, a database that became the foundation of modern computer vision technology, will join AMD as executive vice-president and chief scientist.

Li said in a blog post that “without a focused hardware, AI is hobbled in efficiency”. The two companies partnered last year to train models on AMD’s chips and discovered they were a “natural fit”, she wrote.
AMD invested in World Labs as part of a $1bn fundraising in February that included Nvidia, at a reported $5bn valuation. Andreessen Horowitz is among the start-up’s early backers.

AMD has made acquisitions over recent years as it looks to build its hardware and software ecosystem. These include its $4.4bn acquisition of ZT Systems in 2025 and the $665mn acquisition of Finnish AI model company Silo AI in 2024.

It has also agreed deals to supply chips to leading AI model makers, offering up its equity to secure long-term purchase commitments. In February, AMD struck a multibillion-dollar chip supply deal with Meta, with a provision for the social media group to take up to a 10 per cent stake in the company over time. An October 2025 deal with OpenAI included a similar share arrangement.
AMD announced it would invest up to $5bn in OpenAI’s main rival Anthropic as it commits to buying tens of billions of dollars of AMD’s AI data centre chips.
The World Labs deal comes as AMD and its rivals expect a new phase of massive growth from AI in robotics, with the companies developing specialised chips for these purposes.
The companies are also experimenting with new chip architectures that could start to displace the graphics processing units that dominated the first phase of AI computing.

Nvidia paid $20bn in December 2025 to hire top executives and licence technology from start-up Groq, which developed a specialised accelerator chip aimed at running AI models faster than current hardware. Nvidia incorporated this technology into a new product this year. In August, AMD announced it was acquiring specialised chip company Taalas.

title: Pope Leo criticises Nvidia’s Jensen Huang over AI safety
paragraphs: Michael Actonin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Pope Leo XIV has rebuked Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang for downplaying the risks posed by AI, saying concerns about the threat the technology poses to humanity should be taken seriously.

Huang, along with US President Donald Trump, has rejected calls from frontierAIlabs OpenAI and Anthropic to co-ordinate and slow model development and introduce more regulation following a series of high-profile hacking incidents and public warnings about the technology’s existential risks.
Pope Leo told reporters he had read reports about Nvidia launching new safety tools for model builders on Monday but questioned Huang’s commitment to safety in light of his recent comments.
“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” PopeLeosaid on the flight back to Rome from a visit to France.
“I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously,” he added.
Pope Leo criticises Nvidia chief over AI safety

The Pope’s swipe at the leader of the world’s most valuable company testifies to the extraordinary level of concern around AI safety issues, which have become a top priority for leaders around the world.
OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei appeared at the UN Security Council last week to address the issue and argue for greater global co-operation.

But the push for international action on AI guardrails has been stalled by Trump, who has called warnings that the technology could threaten humanity a “hoax” and rejected any “globalist scheme of control of superintelligence”.
Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump on several occasions, said AI anxiety was not “fake news, as some have said”.
“If someone were to ask me: ‘Am I in panic mode?’ No, I’m not. I sleep at night,” Pope Leo said. “This is a problem that I think we need to sit down and talk about.”

The pontiff’s comment about Nvidia comes after the $5.5tn chipmaker unveiled a new set of security tools aimed at policing the activity of AI agents — bots that can operate autonomously — including a system called “Sentry” that tracks agent behaviour using Nvidia’s “data processing unit” chips.
An Nvidia executive told reporters the tools would have prevented a high-profile hack of Hugging Face in July by OpenAI agents that triggered fresh debate about the risks AI poses.
“It’s interesting to note that, just today, I read that the head of Nvidia claims that he has found some way of inserting into AI certain guardrails,” Pope Leo said.

Since assuming the papacy last year, Chicago-born Pope Leo has shown a close interest in AI. In May heissued a formal letterknown as an “encyclical” in which he said AI was not morally neutral and must be “disarmed” through robust regulation to ensure it serves humanity rather than undermine it.
Last week it emerged that OpenAI’s models had hacked dozens of websites, including an Australian health service website, during the course of routine training runs.

The Nvidia chief has spent recent weeks joining forces with Trump to argue against the need for additional regulation or oversight, emphasising that the responsibility to ensure safety lies with the individual companies.
“The market forces are already there. We don’t need any new laws. We don’t need new regulations,” Huang said earlier this month.
Huang, who has become one of the closest tech executives to Trump, took a call from the president onstage at an event in which he agreed that the concerns amounted to a hoax.
Pope Leo’s intervention comes as leading AI executives are set to meet Trump and US lawmakers at the White House on Tuesday.
Trump dined with Amodei on Sunday night, in a sign of détente with the company after the Pentagon banned its products when Anthropic tried to restrict their use in warfare.
Nvidia declined to comment.

title: Singapore’s bet on chipmaking
paragraphs: Owen Walkerin Singapore
PublishedSeptember 29 2026
Singapore’s ambitions to seize more of the global chip industry are limited only by its size, according to Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Last month Wong announced a project for the city-state to merge several of its smaller islands into a bigger piece of reclaimed land, saying it could “help shape Singapore for the next 50 years” by supporting a new generation of industries, including advanced manufacturing.
While best known as a trading and finance hub,Singaporehas also become a key producer of the semiconductors that drive the global economy.

On Monday VisionPower Semiconductor Manufacturing Company — a joint venture between Taiwan’s Vanguard and Dutch chipmaker NXP — opened its doors on a $7.8bn plant, becoming the latest high-tech company in the country.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, VSMC chair Leuh Fang said the company was even considering opening a second plant in Singapore in order to meet the high levels of demand.
Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

Singapore’s economy has this year been turbocharged by chips and other advanced manufacturing, from medical devices to aerospace components and speciality chemicals. The global AI boom, in particular, has been a boon for its chipmakers.

“Singapore has done very well in becoming an established base for this emerging area of growth,” said Tan Yew Kong, general manager of Asia-Pacific manufacturing at GlobalFoundries, one of the chipmakers in Singapore. “AI is booming and Singapore has an advantage.”

The country makes one in 10 of the world’ssemiconductors— though a smaller share of the most advanced chips — and a fifth of the machinery that makes them, according to the country’s Economic Development Board. The industry accounts for nearly 7 per cent of Singapore’s GDP.

Singapore had its strongest first-half trade performance since 2010, according to Moody’s, and growth has been higher in the two months since. Electronics exports surged 132 per cent in August compared with a year earlier, while shipments of personal computers — including server racks used in data centres — rose 238 per cent.

Between 2022 and 2025, Singapore attracted more than $23.5bn in semiconductor investments. Among the companies that have set up fabrication plants to make chips are Micron, Infineon, Siltronic and UMC. Applied Materials opened a$500mn campusin June.
But the success has brought geopolitical risks. The chip industry is “becoming a security problem”, Tan said.

In March, US trade representative Jamieson Greerbegan an investigationinto several countries over alleged structural excess manufacturing capacity. Singapore’s microchip and electronic equipment industries were highlighted, with the expectation that “Singapore’s trade surplus in the semiconductor supply chain will grow”.

title: Will Adani get an airline?
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 29 2026
This article is an on-site version of the India Business Briefing newsletter. To receive it in your inbox regularly,sign upif you’re a premium subscriber or upgrade your subscriptionhere.

Good morning. This promises to be an eventful week, with the Cockroach Janta Party calling on the country’syouth to protest against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over mass deletions from the electoral rolls. They are timing the march for Mahatma Gandhi’s birth anniversary (since Friday is a public holiday, there will be no India Business Briefing).
In today’s newsletter, the insurance regulator has proposed mega changes to fees and commissions for policy sales. But first, the intrigue and drama around the possible prospect of an Adani Airlines.
TheAdani Groupand the government appear to be engaged in an intricate tango over the group’s airline ambitions.

The issue first surfaced in July, when media reports suggested Adani was seeking a waiver from a rule that prevents the group, as the operator of Mumbai’s main airport, from holding more than 10 per cent of shares in a scheduled airline. At the time, Adani Enterprises, the group flagship company, strongly denied that it had plans to enter the airline business, telling the stock exchanges that reports otherwise were “entirely baseless”. The following day, however, The Economic Times reported that Arun Bansal, chief executive of Adani Airport Holdings, had asked the Airports Authority of India to waive the restriction in a letter on June 4. The letter said group company Adani Defence & Aerospace was evaluating the possibility of starting an airline as a natural extension of its aviation business.

Cut to last week. Speaking at an industry event in Delhi, civil aviation minister Ram Mohan Naidu Kinjarapu said the government was examining the pros and cons of allowing airport operators to run airlines. He said it would be cautious given the conflict of interest that cross-ownership creates, but also made clear it wants more competition in a market where IndiGo and Air India account for more than 90 per cent of domestic traffic. The Times of India last week quoted Bansal saying that “as airport CEO” he would “not like to” compete with his own customers. I asked Adani Enterprises at the weekend about the group’s intentions, but did not hear back in time for this newsletter.

It is worth noting that the restriction itself dates back to the 2006 privatisation of the Mumbai and Delhi airports. It was written into the specific agreements between the government and operators, and is not a blanket rule that is applied to every airport in the country.

IndiGo co-founder and managing director Rahul Bhatia has vehemently opposed any relaxation. Bhatia sees airport operators owning airlines as a “massive conflict of interest”, sincethey control access to critical infrastructuresuch as airport slots and parking bays. He has also pointed out that there is no global precedent for an arrangement he says could ultimately hurt consumers.

Several things are at play here. The government has to tread carefully because the company at the centre of the debate isAdani, one of India’s most high-profile business groups. Any relaxation of a rule that could directly benefit it is therefore likely to attract political scrutiny.
At the same time, the government has a legitimate argument for wanting more competition. BothAir IndiaandIndiGo have had their own troublesin the past year.

The question, then, is whether the government can devise a framework that addresses the conflict-of-interest concerns while allowing new capital into an industry dominated by two groups. It will be interesting to see whether a cabinet decision emerges.

India’s insurance regulator is proposing sweeping changes in the commissions and fees paid to sell policies. In a consultation paper published last week, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) proposed capping payouts to intermediaries and distributors, and reversing its own 2023 decision to free up the commission structure. The caps vary by product type and by the term over which premiums are paid. It is a complicated structure, depending on the nature of the product and the duration of the policy, but roughly the proposed mandate would cut maximum commissions to 15 per cent for life insurers from as high as 26.7 per cent for some, and to 20 per cent for non-life policies from up to 30 per cent.

There are several reasons for the regulator to change its mind on commissions and fees. The sector isopening to foreign capital, and Irdai wants commissions to better reflect business realities. Products with single-premium payments, or those that have tax benefits, basically sell themselves without big incentives. Irdai’s analysis of 2023-25 data found distributor payouts grew 125 per cent, but premiums grew only 28 per cent. This makes it an inefficient incentive structure.

The changes, if implemented, would hit financial services firms whose revenue leans heavily on insurance sales, and large Indian banks, for whom insurance commissions are a sizeable share of retail income — as high as 10 per cent of fee income for some. PB Fintech, the parent of Policybazaar, a listed insurance seller, told analysts its non-life insurance business could lose up to two-thirds of its value if the proposals went through. The company’s stock fell more than 36 per cent on the publication of the consultation paper, erasing over Rs314bn in market capitalisation.

Mouthwatering incentives have fuelled rampant mis-selling, with agents steering clients towards whichever policy pays the highest commission rather than the one that best suits their needs. Irdai’s changes also aim to reward persistence and encourage distributors to keep clients paying premiums rather than lapsing mid-policy. These reforms are expected to make insurance cheaper, though that depends on how much of the savings insurers actually pass on. The Indian insurance industry has grown increasingly customer-unfriendly in recent years, with complaints piling up over denied claims. This is especially true in health insurance, where some insurers’ claim settlement ratio is as low as 82 per cent. The proposed changes should improve the competitive landscape, as sellers will not be incentivised by disproportionate commissions. Feedback on the consultation paper is open until October 25.

This is largely because the country is unable to create enough jobs for its graduates.
