title: Convenience store woman: Lady Gaga urges Japanese to work at FamilyMart
paragraphs: Harry DempseyandLeo Lewisin Tokyo
PublishedSeptember 29 2026
Japanese convenience store chain FamilyMart has enlisted global pop megastar Lady Gaga as it ratchets up its staff recruitment efforts to offset the country’s acute labour shortage.

In a commercial that aired this week, the American singer, clad in a custom navy leather uniform and white platform stilettos, hands outfamichikifried chicken and mops the floors of a monochrome convenience store.

The 30-second spot is the convenience store chain’s latest effort to entice more part-time staff to join its ranks, as Japan’s corporate giants pour increasing resources into advertising budgets and recruitment efforts to battle a nationwide labour shortage.

“Why not work at FamilyMart,” Lady Gaga asks viewers in Japanese as she struts down an aisle past two android-looking versions of herself, restocking shelves with products including cup noodles, snacks and curry packets.
Lady Gaga's FamilyMart advert

“This must be the first time that a convenience store has used a famous celebrity to promote the idea of working there. Usually, the ads are for new products or discount campaigns,” said Masuji Ikeda, senior researcher at the Distribution Economics Institute of Japan. “It’s a turning point.”
Lady Gagais immensely popular in Japan, respectfully dubbed “Gaga-sama” by fans and selling out all six January dates of her Mayhem Ball tour in the country.

Convenience stores and their franchisees, which rely on part-time labour, arestruggling to attract staff, for whom 24/7 operations, low wages and gruelling work offer little appeal, and at a time when a shrinking workforce is beginning to give workers more leverage and inflation is eating into profit margins.
Advertising professionals said the Lady Gaga tie-in reflected a broader shift within corporate Japan.

“More and more [clients] are telling us that the only point of marketing for us is now recruitment,” said an executive at Hakuhodo, one of Japan’s major advertising agencies. “What they need above everything is for people to know their company name so that they will think about working for them.”
They added: “This is advertising for people, because that is what they need most.”

A spokesperson forFamilyMart, which is currently advertising 10,481 part-time jobs across 16,455 stores in Japan, told the FT that the Lady Gaga campaign was the latest in a series of efforts to make its workplace more appealing, fun and exciting to potential jobseekers.
The convenience store chain has refreshed its uniform for the first time in a decade, debuting a more modern, casual style and colour scheme at a catwalk show at Tokyo’s premier sumo venue in August.

Convenience chains have also led the charge onaccepting more foreign workersto fill staffing gaps — one solution to Japan’s demographic crisis that traditional industries have resisted. They have also introduced more technology, necessitating a more tech-savvy workforce.

Family Mart in particular has come under pressure froma sales slowdownover the past year as customer traffic has fallen, which could hamper franchises’ ability to pay higher wages and attract and retain staff.
FamilyMart is the second biggest among Japan’s three leading convenience store chains, with ¥3.3tn ($21bn) of annual revenue.

This year, 7-Eleven, the sector’s largest player, announced the first comprehensive overhaul in half a century of its franchise agreements, lowering the royalties paid to head office and giving franchisees more wriggle room to increase part-time wages.
FamilyMart said it was not working on any such plans. The company declined to comment on the cost of the Lady Gaga campaign.

title: US Treasury threatens crackdown on Wall Street tax-avoidance strategies
paragraphs: PublishedSeptember 28 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?
The US Treasury on Monday took its first concrete steps towards cracking down on a suite of strategies used by wealthy US investors to cut their tax bills.
The department warned that it could clamp down on “potentially abusive” tactics and issued a ruling targeting the aggressive use of ETFs to avoid taxable gains.
It said in a notice it was probing the use of strategies that “purport to produce tax results that may be inconsistent with the purpose and proper application of the relevant federal tax rules”.

In an accompanying ruling, the Internal Revenue Service targeted a strategy known as the 351 conversion, which allows investors with appreciated assets to rebalance their portfolios without incurring taxable gains.
“This is a seismic moment in the ETF market,” said Brent Sullivan, an independent tax analyst and editor of the Tax Alpha Insider newsletter.

Strategies that help wealthy Americans minimise theirtaxbills have surged in popularity in recent years, aided by a US stock market boom that has shifted the focus for some investors towards “tax alpha”, or gains derived from lowering tax liabilities.

Hedge funds offering tax alpha strategies accruedmore than $90bnbetween the start of 2025 and April this year, according to FT calculations. Since 2021, ETFs created using 351 conversions have raised a total of at least $21bn, according to Tax Alpha Insider.

The 351 conversion is one of several strategies that take advantage of the favourable tax treatment ofETFs, which US investors can usually use to avoid paying capital gains tax by trading “in kind” with market makers so that no cash changes hands.
But in a ruling on Monday the IRS said it would treat some of these transactions as taxable exchanges.

“Our message on these conversions is clear: they don’t work under existing law,” Treasury secretary Scott Bessent wrote on X. “Treasury is serious about cracking down on transactions designed to dodge taxes or exploit our federal tax code,” he added.

Sullivan said the ruling targeted cases in which “someone contributes a portfolio of securities that is out of step with the ETF’s prospectus and then quickly washes those securities via in-kind redemption”.
He cautioned: “It’s going to come down to the facts and circumstances of each case” and added that the ruling would not “kill . . . routine tax planning” that involves the 351 conversion.
The Treasury’s notice said it was seeking further information on a series of “strategies used by tax-aware funds” together with a list of ETF manoeuvres including the 351 conversion.

The written notice marks the Treasury’s first escalation since it signalled its interest in probing tax strategies at an industry event in July, where officials warned they would not turn “a blind eye to aggressive planning”.

The Treasury added it was “also considering issuing additional guidance or taking other action to address the transactions described in this notice” and that such guidance could apply “retroactively”.
Shares in Affiliated Managers Group, which owns a stake in AQR, a pioneer of the latest breed of tax-aware investing strategies, fell as much as 2 per cent on Monday.

AQR is, by some estimates, the largest hedge fund in the world. Together with rival Quantinno, it popularised an approach that uses leverage and algorithmic trading to buy and short securities at scale, and to systematically realise losses on positions.
AQR said previously that the “primary draw for investors” should be the returns from its strategies — the “pre-tax alpha”, or market-beating performance — before any tax benefits.

Strategies that help wealthy Americans minimise theirtaxbills have surged in popularity in recent years, aided by a US stock market boom that has shifted the focus for some investors towards “tax alpha”, or gains derived from lowering tax liabilities.

Hedge funds offering tax alpha strategies accruedmore than $90bnbetween the start of 2025 and April this year, according to FT calculations. Since 2021, ETFs created using 351 conversions have raised a total of at least $21bn, according to Tax Alpha Insider.

The 351 conversion is one of several strategies that take advantage of the favourable tax treatment ofETFs, which US investors can usually use to avoid paying capital gains tax by trading “in kind” with market makers so that no cash changes hands.

But in a ruling on Monday the IRS said it would treat some of these transactions as taxable exchanges.

“Our message on these conversions is clear: they don’t work under existing law,” Treasury secretary Scott Bessent wrote on X. “Treasury is serious about cracking down on transactions designed to dodge taxes or exploit our federal tax code,” he added.

Sullivan said the ruling targeted cases in which “someone contributes a portfolio of securities that is out of step with the ETF’s prospectus and then quickly washes those securities via in-kind redemption”.

He cautioned: “It’s going to come down to the facts and circumstances of each case” and added that the ruling would not “kill . . . routine tax planning” that involves the 351 conversion.

The Treasury’s notice said it was seeking further information on a series of “strategies used by tax-aware funds” together with a list of ETF manoeuvres including the 351 conversion.

The written notice marks the Treasury’s first escalation since it signalled its interest in probing tax strategies at an industry event in July, where officials warned they would not turn “a blind eye to aggressive planning”.

The Treasury added it was “also considering issuing additional guidance or taking other action to address the transactions described in this notice” and that such guidance could apply “retroactively”.

Shares in Affiliated Managers Group, which owns a stake in AQR, a pioneer of the latest breed of tax-aware investing strategies, fell as much as 2 per cent on Monday.

AQR is, by some estimates, the largest hedge fund in the world. Together with rival Quantinno, it popularised an approach that uses leverage and algorithmic trading to buy and short securities at scale, and to systematically realise losses on positions.

AQR said previously that the “primary draw for investors” should be the returns from its strategies — the “pre-tax alpha”, or market-beating performance — before any tax benefits.

title: OpenAI axes next model citing safety issues
paragraphs: Ryan McMorrowandGeorge Hammondin San Francisco
PublishedSeptember 29 2026

OpenAI has pulled the release of its next AI model, saying it performed worse than its predecessor on safety evaluations as the industry grapples with a spate of incidents in which AI agents hacked into other companies and governments.
Saachi Jain, head of safety systems atOpenAI, said the company decided to hold back GPT-6.1 Astra after the model “didn’t quite meet the bar” for staying within the bounds of its instructions.

The announcement comes after OpenAI last week said it had notified dozens of partners, including governments, that its AI agents had breached their systems and that agents had inadvertently leaked more than 50 images shared by users to image-hosting sites.
This marked the latest in a series of disclosures about misbehaviour and hacking by OpenAI’s AI agents — bots that can perform complex tasks autonomously.
The $852bn start-up has acknowledged that in some cases it took months to detect agents that had run amok during internal model training and testing.
Chief executive Sam Altman has joined industry calls to slow the pace of research to ensure AI is developed safely and has said the company has already changed the way it trains models.
Jain said OpenAI faced a “trade-off” between making models persistent enough to complete tasks and ensuring they follow their instructions, a concept known as “alignment”.

“You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope, but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction,” Jain said in a statement.
She said GPT-6.1 Astra “didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done”.
“When we ship [our models] to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment,” she added.

A person close to the company said GPT-6.1 Astra had scored below GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s current most advanced model, on alignment evaluations but the company had other models coming soon that met its safety bar. The Wall Street Journal first reported the OpenAI decision.

OpenAI has been reviewing its models’ behaviour during training and evaluation since an incident that came to light in July, in which agents gained access to the internet during testing and hacked into Hugging Face, the AI model and data repository.

The review has so far unearthed several other incidents, including agents hacking an Australian government health service website. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Wednesday called the breach, and OpenAI’s slow response to it, “obviously unacceptable”.

Security breaches at OpenAI and rivals Anthropic and Google have prompted renewed calls for an industry-wide pause or slowdown. Altman joined Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and SpaceX’s Elon Musk in calls to “pace the frontier” of AI development so that safety measures can keep up.

But President Donald Trump has resisted calls to regulate the sector or impose strict guardrails on leading US labs, arguing that American primacy in the technology is vital to staying ahead of China.
Additional reporting by Rafe Rosner-Uddin

title: Anthropic warns of ‘existential risks to humanity’ in IPO prospectus
paragraphs: George Hammondin San Francisco andJames Fontanella-Khanin New York
PublishedSeptember 29 2026
UpdatedSeptember 29 2026
Could you be the FT’s top trader?

Anthropic has formally warned investors that its technology may pose “existential risks to humanity” in a long-awaited initial public offering prospectus circulated with a small group of partners in recent days.

The nearly $1tn AI start-up led by Dario Amodei devoted almost a third of its lengthy S1 filing to detailing “risk factors”, including the potential of increasingly advanced AI models to manipulate, blackmail and exhibit other unpredictable behaviours.

Anthropic outlined more prosaic risks, including the extreme concentration of its customer base, with close to a quarter of revenue last year coming from just two clients, according to people familiar with the filing.

The extraordinary warnings in its risk disclosures add to the challenge faced by public markets investors in valuing the leading US AI group when it launches what is expected to be the most highly valued IPO of all time.
The Claude maker also provided investors with a clearer picture of the challenging economics of building state of the art AI models ahead of the listing, expected on the Nasdaq this autumn.
Anthropic said it plans to spend $518bn on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming years to support its rapid growth.

The AI lab’s backers are confident Anthropic can list at a valuation of over $2tn, more than double the level achieved in its last funding round in May and beyond the $1.78tn achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June. They point to its extraordinary growth rate to justify their bullishness.
But concerns about the risks posed by AI now threaten to dim that optimism after current and former Anthropic staff came out with public warnings that runaway AI could end humanity within a decade.
Amodei told the UN Security Council last week that AI could threaten humankind and was “the most important global security issue facing the world today”.

The Anthropic chief has this month led public calls for “pacing the frontier” of AI development. His arch-rival at OpenAI, Sam Altman, along with Musk, backed Amodei’s proposals for industry co-operation to slow development and enhance safety measures, in a rare moment of unity.

Safety concerns have increased following a series of high-profile cyber security incidents in which AI ‘agents’ have breached external systems. Last week, OpenAI revealed its tools hadhacked “dozens”of external sites, including governments.
The ChatGPT maker on Mondayscrapped plansto release its newest model next month, citing safety concerns.

Anthropic’s prospectus also revealed details of its prior financial performance and governance arrangements, which were first reported by Reuters and confirmed to the FT by multiple people who have seen the filing.
Anthropic declined to comment.

The company recorded an operating loss of more than $8bn last year as it jacked up spending on computing power, Anthropic told investors. Its revenue jumped twelvefold to almost $4.6bn last year. But mounting costs for computing resources to train and run its models pushed operating expenses to almost $13bn.
The group has inked deals to secure computing power from partners including Google, SpaceX and a series of smaller companies.

Anthropic’s spending and revenue have both increased sharply this year. Revenue in the second quarter of this year was $11.5bn, and it is on course for its second consecutive quarter ofoperating profit, albeit on an adjusted basis.
